evidence.text: The Pythagorean theorem, attributed to the ancient Greek mathematician Pythagoras, states that in a right-angled triangle, the square of the hypotenuse (the side opposite the right angle) equals the sum of the squares of the other two sides: a squared plus b squared equals c squared. It is widely used in geometry, construction, navigation, and physics to calculate distances and verify right angles.

Albert Einstein's theory of relativity comprises special relativity (1905) and general relativity (1915). Special relativity establishes that the laws of physics are the same for all non-accelerating observers and that the speed of light in a vacuum is constant, leading to time dilation and length contraction at high speeds. General relativity describes gravity not as a force but as the curvature of spacetime caused by mass and energy. It predicts phenomena such as gravitational lensing, black holes, and the expansion of the universe.

evidence.document_title: Gravity and Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
evidence.text: Newton's law of universal gravitation states that every point mass attracts every other point mass with a force proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. This explains planetary orbits, tides, and why objects fall toward Earth. Gravity is the weakest of the four fundamental forces but dominates at large scales because it is always attractive and has infinite range.

The Fibonacci sequence is a series of numbers where each number is the sum of the two preceding ones, typically starting 0, 1, 1, 2, 3, 5, 8, 13, 21, and so on. Named after the Italian mathematician Fibonacci, the sequence appears in various natural phenomena, such as the arrangement of leaves, flower petals, and spiral shells, and is closely related to the golden ratio.

Geometry is the branch of mathematics concerned with the properties and relationships of points, lines, shapes, and space. Basic concepts include angles, triangles, circles, and polygons, along with formulas for calculating perimeter, area, and volume. Euclidean geometry, based on axioms laid out by the ancient Greek mathematician Euclid, forms the foundation of most introductory geometry taught today.

Electromagnetism is the branch of physics dealing with the electromagnetic force, one of the four fundamental forces of nature. It unifies electricity and magnetism, described by Maxwell's equations. Moving electric charges generate magnetic fields, and changing magnetic fields induce electric currents. This principle underlies technologies such as electric motors, generators, transformers, and wireless communication. Light itself is an electromagnetic wave, spanning a spectrum from radio waves to gamma rays.
